title: Define Your Creative Purpose
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Potkalitsky takes his 'Principle of Purpose' for AI-responsive education and turns it into a concrete lesson for a ninth-grade English unit on The Other Wes Moore. Drawing on Design Tech's 'creative purpose' curriculum, Ross Wehner's argument that purpose should come before content, and rhetorical theory, he proposes that students help redefine what school is for in the age of generative AI. The lesson has students build a 'Purpose Shield' with purpose statements for the class, the school year and high school, then use those purposes in self-led conferences. He suggests teachers complete their own purpose work alongside students. The piece is curriculum design: a plan and rationale for organising learning around student purpose.
points: Wehner's ordering, purpose first and skills second, lets students see why particular skills matter amid rapid technological change.
The Purpose Shield lesson turns abstract purpose into three time-bounded statements (class, year, high school) with symbolic art.
Purpose is treated as collaborative, tested and revised through interaction with others' purposes.
Student purposes feed self-led conferences, giving students ownership of an evaluation process they usually experience as outsiders.
Teachers should model the work by doing their own purpose exercise alongside students.
quotes: Here, the order of things is most significant. Purpose comes first and allows students to recognize and identify the skills that are necessary to realize a particular pathway and outcome.

Wehner’s talk could not be anymore relevant to this particular moment when new technologies are rapidly outmoding existing skill-sets, competencies, and literacies. Wehner’s approach opens up two productive responses to student inquiries about the utility of particular foci within instructional settings.

In the context of my own work, I conceive of purpose as less an individualistic enterprise, and more of a collaborative effort where one’s purpose is constantly tested, refined, revised, and extended through interaction with the purposes of others. The sooner our students learn this important lesson, the better—and with enough forethought and skill, we can successfully model this interactivity in the classroom and across the curriculum.

I think students can sense when their instructors are also engaged in the work continuous the work of purpose-orientation—as opposed to just assigning it in class. I’d recommend that teachers create a Purpose Shield alongside their students in the spirit of Collaboration that undergirds the Principle of Purpose.

In this way, students will take greater ownership over a process in which they usually disempowered and under the evaluative gaze of the “other.” I had the good fortune to work at a vibrant Montessori Middle School for several years over a decade ago, and we found that empowering students through self-led conferences lifted the entire school community into a higher state of engagement, purpose-orientation, grace and civility, and curiosity and inquiry.
